name: Bariai
confidence_why: The only first-hand description, Gallagher & Baehr's 2005 grammar sketch (the same analysis as Gallagher's 2001 phonology data, condensed to "normally penultimate" in Gallagher's 2008 dictionary), puts stress on the penultimate syllable of the stem with morphologically and vowel-height conditioned shifts, Thurston's 1987 survey note that stress is usually penultimate in isolation agrees with it, and Friederici's 1912 remark that the accent is weak and variable is too old and impressionistic to unsettle it.

catalog_quote: A stressed syllable in Bariai is characterised by intensity and a slightly higher pitch than an unstressed syllable. Although stress is not entirely predictable, it is not contrastive in any example found in the data. Stress primarily occurs on the penultimate syllable of the stem. The stress is retained by this syllable regardless of any reduplication or inflectional suffixing. ... (49) /mɑtɑ-g/ [ˈmɑ.tɑk] ‘my eye’ /i-mɑtɑ/ [i.ˈmɑ.tɑ] ‘his eye’ /mɑtɑ-dɑ/ [ˈmɑ.tɑ.dɑ] ‘our (incl) eyes’ When the derivational suffix /-ŋɑ/ appears on a stem, stress is placed on the penultimate syllable of the resulting surface form. (50) /nɑ-kɑdo/ [nɑ.ˈkɑ.do] ‘I do’ /kɑdo-ŋɑ/ [kɑ.ˈdo.ŋɑ] ‘deed’ ... A final high vowel on the stems of inalienably-possessed nouns is always dropped in the 3rd singular form (§1.3), yet the stress always remains on the penultimate syllable of the underlying form. ... Stress shifts from the penultimate syllable to the antepenultimate syllable if the vowel of the latter is lower in height than the former or is the same vowel. (57) /i-tekiɑ/ [i.ˈtɛ.ki.ɑ] ‘its sap’ ... /bolomɑ/ [ˈbo.lo.mɑ] ‘near’ ... If a sequence of two repeated syllables occurs in a three syllable root, stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable. ... In addition to the few words presented in example (46) in which stress is placed on the final syllable, the following examples show that the stress placement is not entirely predictable. (59) /pɑgege/ [pɑ.ˈɣe.ɣe] ‘you (sg) shut’ ...

new_statements.quote: The non-low vowels i, e, o and u are desyllabified when they occur immediately before or after any vowel that is of a lower height. This produces nearly all possible sequences of vowel onglides and offglides. Stress is normally placed upon the penultimate syllable, but see Gallagher & Baehr (2005:9-25) for a more complete description of stress placement and of the phonology.
new_statements.citation: Gallagher, Steve. 2008. Bariai Dictionary, First Corrected Edition. West New Britain Province, Papua New Guinea. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics (ISBN 9980-0-2372-4), introduction, section 'Bariai alphabet and pronunciation'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable; syllable count is affected by glide formation (non-low vowels next to a lower vowel become non-syllabic on/offglides). The fuller account of stress placement is deferred to Gallagher & Baehr 2005 pp. 9-25, which could not be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'normally' and the pointer to Gallagher & Baehr (2005:9-25) for 'a more complete description of stress placement'. Friederici 1912: 172 (single informant, 1908) says the accent is weak and variable, the same word being heard with different accent or double stress, and that compounding, emphasis and question intonation shift the accent. Thurston 1987: 34 (comparative, all NW New Britain languages incl. Bariai/Kabana): 'for words pronounced in isolation, stress is usually penultimate in all languages', stress in running speech not worked out.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, dictionary citation forms; Thurston's corroborating remark is explicitly about words pronounced in isolation. Gallagher states Bariai has no sub-dialects (2008: v).
new_statements.identity_note: Bariai [bch], glottocode bari1286; called Kabana by Thurston (1987) and Barriai by Friederici (1912). Gallagher 2008: v states the language has no sub-dialects (minor lexical pronunciation variants in Kokopo/Gurisi/Akonga). Friederici's 1912 sketch rests on a single informant (Kabui of Kumartantan) interviewed aboard ship. Do not confuse with Lusi/Kaliai (lusi1242) or Kilenge/Maleu (kile1243), which are the comparanda in Goulden 1982/1996; Goulden's 'antepenultimate stress' remark concerns Kilenge, not Bariai.

Note that stress placement on the final syllable is an irregularity.'; §1.6.2 Stress p. 22 'A stressed syllable in Bariai is characterised by intensity and a slightly higher pitch than an unstressed syllable. Although stress is not entirely predictable…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Gallagher 2008: 'Stress is normally placed upon the penultimate syllable') and with the webcat record's current classification morphological, whose citation is already this work. Adds: the domain is the stem (stress stays on the stem penult under inflectional suffixes and prefixes, so the word-level penult is not always stressed), the /-ŋɑ/ derivational exception, the vowel-height and repeated-syllable antepenult retraction, non-contrastiveness, final-stress irregularities, and a list of unpredictable residues.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem and stays there under prefixation, reduplication and inflectional suffixation (e.g. /mɑtɑ-g/ [ˈmɑ.tɑk], /i-mɑtɑ/ [i.ˈmɑ.tɑ], /mɑtɑ-dɑ/ [ˈmɑ.tɑ.dɑ]; /tini-g/ [ˈtɪ.nɪk], /i-tini/ [i.ˈtɪn] where the stem-final high vowel is dropped yet stress stays on the underlying penult). The derivational suffix /-ŋɑ/ is different: stress goes to the penult of the derived surface form (/kɑdo-ŋɑ/ [kɑ.ˈdo.ŋɑ]). Within the stem, stress retracts to the antepenult when the antepenult vowel is lower than, or identical to, the penult vowel (/i-lɑborɑ/ [i.ˈlɑ.βo.rɑ], /bolomɑ/ [ˈbo.lo.mɑ], /ɡiniu/ [ˈgi.ni.u]), and when a three-syllable root ends in two repeated syllables (/ɡiɡimɑ/ [ˈɣi.ɣi.mɑ], /pɑlele/ [ˈpɑ.le.le]). Stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No prose statement. One transcription carries a secondary-stress mark: (59) /i-mɑd-mɑdid/ [i.ˌmɑd.mɑ.ˈdiɾ] 'he is standing' (p. 24), secondary on the reduplicant, primary on the final syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) Final-syllable stress in a few words, called 'an irregularity' (§1.6.1 p. 22): /imɑdid/ [i.mɑ.ˈdiːɾ], /tiŋɑŋɑr/ [ti.ŋɑ.ˈŋɑːr], /sulem/ [su.ˈleːm], /ikɑpir/ [i.kɑ.ˈpiːɾ]; these stressed utterance-final closed syllables are lengthened. (b) 'the following examples show that the stress placement is not entirely predictable' (p. 24): /pɑɡeɡe/ [pɑ.ˈɣe.ɣe], /bɑbɑŋɑ/ [βɑ.ˈβɑ.ŋɑ], /kɑdeŋe/ [kɑ.ˈde.ŋe] (penult where the height/repeated-syllable rules would predict antepenult), /dibɑlɑ/ [ˈdi.βɑ.lɑ] (antepenult with a higher antepenult vowel), /tibur/ [ti.ˈβur], /suluɡ/ [su.ˈluk], /muliɑn/ [ˈmu.li.ɑn]. (c) Vowel length is non-contrastive.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works describe Bariai [bch] of Gloucester District, West New Britain (villages Gurisi, Kokopo, Akonga, Bambak, Namaramanga, Mareka, Alaido), based on Gallagher's 7+ years in the language. The 2005 sketch §1.7 says the language is 'essentially homogeneous', noting only a few lexical pronunciation differences between eastern (Kokopo, Gurisi) and western villages, none concerning stress. Not Lusi/Kaliai or Kilenge/Maleu.

new_statements.relation_note: Corroborates the 2005 sketch (which the webcat record already cites) and the 2008 dictionary's 'normally penultimate': stem-penult with retention under inflection, height-conditioned antepenult retraction, non-contrastive, unpredictable residue. It is the earlier draft of the same author's analysis, so it is not an independent source.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Same analysis as Gallagher & Baehr 2005 in nearly the same words: stress on the penultimate syllable of the stem, kept there under reduplication and inflectional suffixation (oaga [ˈo̯ɑ.ɣɑ], oagaeai [ˈo̯ɑ.ɣɑ.e̯ɑi̯]; matag [ˈmɑ.tɑk], imata [i.ˈmɑ.tɑ], matada [ˈmɑ.tɑ.ɖɑ]); derivational -nga puts stress on the surface penult (kadonga [kʰɑ.ˈɖo.ŋɑ]); stress 'may shift' to the antepenult when that vowel is lower than or the same as the penult vowel (itekia, ilabora, gigima, boloma, buobuo, giniu, iriau, palele, parere, bagele). Non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No prose statement; one transcription with a secondary-stress mark: imadmadid [i.ˌmɑɖ.mɑ.ˈɖiɖ̥] 'he is standing' (p. 4).
new_statements.exceptions: 'Counter examples' listed p. 4: kadenge [kʰɑ.ˈde.ŋe], pagege [pʰɑ.ˈɣe.ɣe], babanga [βɑ.ˈβɑ.ŋɑ], dibala [ˈdi.βɑ.lɑ], ikilele [i.ˈkʰi.le.le], imadmadid [i.ˌmɑɖ.mɑ.ˈɖiɖ̥], tibur [tʰi.ˈβur], sulug [su.ˈluk], mulian [ˈmu.li.ɑn]. Unlike the 2005 sketch, the OPD has no separate repeated-syllable rule (gigima/palele/parere are placed under the vowel-height rule) and lists ikilele as a counter-example rather than as a regular case; final-stress items (tibur, sulug, imadmadid) are simply counter-examples, not called 'an irregularity' tied to lengthening.

The 2005 sketch §1.7 says the language is 'essentially homogeneous', noting only a few lexical pronunciation differences between eastern (Kokopo, Gurisi) and western villages, none concerning stress. Not Lusi/Kaliai or Kilenge/Maleu.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Neither listed work was marked silent or not opened, so I spot-checked the other on-disk sources from the earlier check (all under: Goulden 1982 MA thesis: a full-text search for stress/accent/penult hits only 'they prefer to stress the differences' (non-linguistic sense); no stress statement, silent stands. Goulden 1996 (PL C-135): the only hit, 'This prefix can take the regular antepenultimate stress, e.g. naa-pe a paddle', is in §5.1.1 on the Kilenge na- nominal prefix, not Bariai; already says so. Thurston 1987 p. 34 (p. 42): 'Stress patterns in running speech have not been worked out in detail for most of the languages, but for words pronounced in isolation, stress is usually penultima…

readall_conflicts: antepenult retraction conditioned by vowel height; non-contrastive; a residue of unpredictable words and a few final-stressed words). The two differ only in bookkeeping: the 2005 sketch states the retraction as categorical ('Stress shifts'), adds a separate repeated-syllable rule (gigima, palele, parere, ikilele) and calls final stress 'an irregularity' linked to utterance-final lengthening; the 2001 OPD says 'may shift', folds those items into the height rule and lists ikilele and the final-stressed words among the counter-examples. Gallagher 2008 (the catalog's existing statement) gives only 'normally penultimate' and defers to the 2005 sketch; that word-level phrasing understates the stem domain (e.g. [ˈmɑ.tɑ.dɑ] 'our eyes' is antepenult at word level but stem-penult). the first is a mild disagreement with Gallagher's stable stem-penult, the second is compatible.
